DISCUSSION, DECISION AND REASONS THEREON:
23. I have heard the arguments addressed by the Ld. APP for state and the Ld. Counsel for the accused and carefully perused the documents on record. 
State Vs. Sunil Kumar PS Kamla Market 24. In order to ensure seamless appraisal of evidence, the court has framed following point of determination :
1. Whether the accused Sunil Kumar on 17.11.2013, at about 08.30 am, at Ajmeri Gate Chowk, Delhi was driving a DTC bus bearing registration No. DL1PC9479 without a valid badge, and in a rash and negligent manner so as to endanger human life and safety and in consequence of the same, hit the pedestrian, namely, Heera Mani who was crossing the road and caused his death in consequence of the same.
25. The onus to prove the above point of determination shall be on the prosecution. The prosecution must establish that (1) The alleged vehicle was being driven rashly and negligently. (2) The alleged State vs Sunil Kumar on 17 September, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16669663/
8 vehicle was being driven by the accused. (3) The act of the accused caused death of the deceased Heera Mani. 
(4) The accused was driving the said vehicle without a valid badge. 
26. In order to ensure convenience and avoid repetition of evidence, the first and the third issues are being discussed simultaneously. 
Hence, the issue for determination is whether the said vehicle was being driven rashly and negligently and in consequence of the same, it caused death of the deceased Heera Mani.
27. In order to prove the said point of determination, the factum of rashness and negligence has to be gathered from the surrounding of circumstances. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Ravi Kapoor vs.
State of Rajasthan [Crl. Appeal No. 1838/2009 ] inter alia held as under:
"In order to examine the merit or otherwise of contentions (b) and (c) raised on behalf of the appellant, it is necessary for the Court to first and foremost State Vs.
Sunil Kumar PS Kamla Market examine (a) what is rash and negligent driving; and (b) whether it can be gathered from the attendant circumstances. Rash and negligent driving has to be examined in light of the facts and circumstances of a given case. It is a fact incapable of being construed or seen in isolation. It must be examined in light of the attendant circumstances. A person who drives a vehicle on the road is liable to be held responsible for the act as well as for the result. It may not be always possible to determine with reference to the speed of a vehicle whether a person was driving rashly and negligently. Both these acts presuppose an abnormal conduct. Even when one is driving a vehicle at a slow speed but recklessly and negligently, it would amount to 'rash and negligent driving' within the meaning of the language of Section 279 IPC. That is why the legislature has used the words 'manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life'. The preliminary conditions, thus, are that (a) it is the manner in which the vehicle is driven; (b) it be driven either rashly or negligently;
and (c) such rash or negligent driving should be such as to endanger human life.
Once these ingredients are satisfied, the penalty contemplated under Section 279 IPC is attracted.
'Negligence' means omission to do something which a reasonable and prudent person guided by the considerations which ordinarily regulate human affairs would do or doing something which a prudent and reasonable person guided by similar considerations would not do. Negligence is not an absolute term but is a relative one;
it is rather a comparative term. It is difficult to state with precision any mathematically exact formula by which negligence or lack of it can be infallibly measured in a given case. Whether there exists negligence per se or the course of conduct amounts to negligence will normally depend upon the attending and surrounding facts and circumstances which have to be taken into consideration by the Court. In a given case, even not doing what one was ought to do can constitute State vs Sunil Kumar on 17 September, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16669663/
9 negligence.
The Court has to adopt another parameter, i.e., 'reasonable care' in determining the question of negligence or contributory negligence. The doctrine of reasonable care imposes an obligation or a duty upon a person (for example a driver) to care for the pedestrian on the road and this duty attains a higher degree when the pedestrian happen to be children of tender years. It is axiomatic to say that while driving a vehicle on a public way, there is an implicit duty cast on the drivers to see that their driving does not endanger the life of the right users of the road, may be either vehicular users or pedestrians. They are expected to take sufficient care to avoid danger to others".
